overview: This review sim is about low-speed aircraft handling and the discipline that keeps you ahead of the airplane when energy is low and stall margin is small. Be ready to brief the Three Cs, talk through Slow Flight and SCATSAFE cleanly, manage total energy between maneuvers, and explain when a slip helps versus hurts.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The Three Cs are the setup discipline that protects every stall-series or low-speed maneuver. A good brief makes them sound automatic, not optional.

children.text: Configuration: put the aircraft in the correct setup for the maneuver before you start chasing cues later.
Checklist: complete the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist over the ICS.
Clear area: use visual scan, TCAS, and clearing turns as required to make sure the working area is safe.
The Three Cs may be accomplished in any order.
If maneuvers are flown in a series, you do not have to repeat them between every setup unless the situation changes.
Use an approximately 180-degree clearing turn with 30 to 60 degrees of bank, with 45 degrees AOB maximum in the landing configuration.
Recover any stall maneuver above 6000 feet AGL.

items.text: Slow Flight is where you prove you can keep the T-6B coordinated, trimmed, and under control in a near-stalled condition instead of just surviving the setup.

children.text: Complete the maneuver above 6000 feet AGL.
Slow below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, and complete the Before Landing Checklist plus the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist.
Clear the working area, lower flaps to LDG, continue decelerating to about 85 KIAS, and set power at about 45 percent torque.
Fly a coordinated, level 30-degree AOB turn for about 180 degrees of heading, then reverse with another 30-degree AOB turn back to the original heading.
Add power and trim as required to hold altitude and airspeed while keeping the ball centered.
Expect the stick shaker to be on throughout the maneuver.
Advance PCL to MAX, confirm below 150 KIAS, raise the gear, move the flaps from LDG to TO, then retract the flaps at 110 KIAS minimum.
Keep trimming during the recovery so the aircraft accelerates cleanly instead of wallowing out of the maneuver.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft is accelerating back toward cruise, re-trimmed, and balanced instead of still fighting leftover control pressures.
Poor trim use usually becomes poor altitude and heading control.
Students also get behind the aircraft by trying to run checklists in the middle of maneuvering instead of before the setup is stabilized.

items.text: SCATSAFE is the instructor-demonstrated low-speed handling lesson. The goal is understanding what the airplane is telling you near stall, not memorizing the acronym without knowing why each piece matters.

children.text: Complete the maneuver above 6000 feet AGL.
Slow below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, and complete the Before Landing Checklist plus the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist.
Clear the area, lower flaps to LDG, slow to about 80 KIAS or 15 units AOA, and set power at about 45 percent torque.
Straight and level: recognize the back side of the power curve and the sight picture that matches rotation or just prior to touchdown.
Coordination exercise: use small bank changes with coordinated rudder and feel how much rudder the aircraft really needs at low speed.
Adverse yaw: see how the nose wanders when rudder is missing and how much cleaner the rollout looks when coordination is correct.

Torque and turns, steep turns, abrupt control movement, flap retraction, and effectiveness of controls all reinforce the same lesson: low-speed flight punishes abrupt inputs and poor coordination quickly.
The maneuver is complete when the demo has shown each low-speed effect clearly and the aircraft is recovered to a stable, coordinated flight condition.
The stick shaker may be on throughout the maneuver.
Common errors are abrupt control movements, failure to clear the area, poor altitude control, and inadequate trim.

items.text: Energy management is what turns a collection of maneuvers into a smooth profile. You should be able to explain total energy, how to gain or lose it, and how that changes what maneuver makes sense next.

children.text: Total energy is airspeed plus altitude. A simple rule of thumb is that 1000 feet of altitude is worth about 50 knots with MAX power and the canopy bow on the horizon.
A practical working state for maneuvering is usually 180 to 200 KIAS at a mid-area altitude, because that lets you trade into most briefed entry parameters with only a small adjustment.
Lose energy with low power, more drag, or higher AOA. Gain energy with MAX power, low AOA, and climbs in the 140 to 160 KIAS range.
A strong answer connects energy planning to sortie flow: sequence maneuvers to minimize repositioning and avoid wasting time rebuilding airspeed or altitude you did not need to throw away.
If you are constantly surprised by your energy state, you are already behind the aircraft.

items.text: A slip is an out-of-balance maneuver used to lose altitude and increase sink rate while holding a desired ground track. You should understand when it is useful and what makes it easy to mishandle.

children.text: The normal demo setup is a slip to high key at 125 KIAS in the clean configuration.
It may also be demonstrated at 120 KIAS with gear down and flaps as required.
Use power as required to hold the briefed airspeed while the slip is established and unloaded.
Announce the slip clearly: left or right wing down, left or right top rudder.
From wings level, lower one wing and apply opposite rudder while adjusting bank and rudder to maintain the desired track.
From a turn, lower the inboard wing and increase opposite rudder pressure, then keep adjusting both to hold the ground track.
Monitor airspeed closely, use nose attitude to hold it, and expect a rate of descent that may exceed 2000 feet per minute.
Take out the slip smoothly with 200 to 300 feet remaining so you can arrest the sink rate and ensure positive control before the final part of the maneuver.
The maneuver is complete when the wings are level, rudder pressure is relaxed, the descent is under control, and the aircraft is back on a stable flight path instead of still unloading the slip.
Stall speed increases in the slip, and stability is reduced even more with gear down.
If full rudder is used, remain below 150 KIAS.
The low-fuel light for the low-wing tank may illuminate regardless of actual fuel state.

studyNotes.summary: Treat this as a low-speed handling review: configuration discipline, coordinated control inputs, energy awareness, and smooth recoveries all have to connect.

summary: Three Cs, Slow Flight, SCATSAFE, Energy Management, and Slip as a low-speed handling review.
title: Low-Speed Handling and Energy Management
